'''Blaine Francis Nye''' (born March 29, 1946) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[Lineman (gridiron football)#Offensive line|offensive lineman]] for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford Cardinal]], known then as the Indians.

==Early life==
Nye was born March 29, 1946, in [[Ogden, Utah]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Blaine Nye Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/N/NyexBl00.htm |access-date=2025-12-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> His father Blaine Sr. was a career [[United States Marine Corps|United States Marine]], who served as a [[gunnery sergeant]] at [[Marine Corps Air Station El Toro|El Toro Marine Air Station]] in Nye's youth.<ref name=":1" />

Nye played [[high school football|football]] at [[Servite High School]] in [[Anaheim, California]], and graduated in 1964.<ref name="servhsasp">{{cite web |url=https://www.servitehs.org/page.cfm?p=1357 |publisher=Servite High School |location=Anaheim, California |agency=Alumni Spotlight |title=Blaine Nye |access-date=March 8, 2023}}</ref> He was a [[two-way player]] on the school's [[High school football|football team]] for three years. He was a 170 lb (77.1 kg) or 190 lb (86.2 kg) starting tackle as a sophomore in 1961.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lucero |first=John |date=October 26, 1961 |title=Mater Dei, Servite Clash For First Time At Bowl |work=The Register (Santa Ana, California) |pages=B14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=October 21, 1961 |title=Servite Battle St. Paul Tonight |work=Anaheim Bulletin (Anaheim, California) |pages=C-2}}</ref> He was a 210 lb (95.3 kg) tackle as a junior in 1962, and was named first-team All-[[Trinity League|Angelus League]] at both [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]] and [[defensive tackle]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 29, 1962 |title=Mater Dei Puts 11 On All-Angelus |work=The Register (Santa Ana, California) |pages=B14}}</ref> By his senior year (1963) he was 230 lb (104.3 kg). Servite had an 8–1 record, losing only to the Angelus League champions ([[Mater Dei High School (Santa Ana, California)|Mater Dei]]).<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=West |first=Eddie |date=April 30, 1964 |title=West Winds, Stanford Gets Servite's Blaine Nye |work=The Register (Santa Ana, California) |pages=B14}}</ref> That year he was first-team All-Angelus League at defensive tackle and second team All-[[Orange County, California|Orange County]] at offensive tackle.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=November 22, 1963 |title=Carrillo, Lawrence Named County's Top Players |work=The Bulletin (Anaheim, California) |pages=C-3}}</ref> He was also lineman of the week five times with Servite.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |date=July 23, 1964 |title=Studying The Stars |work=The Register (Santa Ana, California) |pages=B13}}</ref> He appeared in the August 1964 Orange County Prep All-Star Game at tackle.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=West |first=Eddie |date=August 13, 1964 |title=West Winds, Expect 8000 For All-Star |work=The Register (Santa Ana, California) |pages=B12}}</ref> 

Nye also played [[Center (basketball)|center]] on Servite's [[High school basketball|basketball]] team, that won a championship.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Vollman |first=Tim |date=December 13, 1963 |title=Orange Defeats Servite, Friars Fight For Third |work=The Bulletin (Anaheim, California) |pages=C2}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> As a 6 ft 4 in (1.93 m) senior at center, he was named second-team All-Angelus League.<ref>{{Cite news |date=February 28, 1964 |title=Juniors Dominate All-Angelus Team |work=The Bulletin (Anaheim, California) |pages=C2}}</ref> He was also an over .300 hitter on the school's [[baseball]] team, playing [[First baseman|first base]].<ref name=":1" /> 

Nye was an honor student, and graduated as his class [[valedictorian]] in 1964, No. 1 in his class. In 1979, Servite honored him with a Blaine Nye Night.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 18, 1979 |title=Servite-St. Paul Vie on Blaine Nye Night |work=The Los Angeles Times |pages=18, Part III}}</ref><ref name=":1" />

== College career ==
Nye was pursued by the [[United States Naval Academy]] and other colleges, but he accepted an academic scholarship from [[Stanford University]], where he would also play football under head coach [[John Ralston (American football)|John Ralston]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> He was a starting tackle on the freshman team in 1964.<ref name=":4" /> As a 235 lb (106.6 kg) sophomore in [[1965 Stanford Indians football team|1965]], Nye began the season at [[defensive end]], but Ralston moved him to [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]] as part of an effort to improve the offense.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gamage |first=Walt |date=October 1, 1965 |title=Cards expect aerial attack |work=Palo Alto Times (Palo Alto, California) |pages=24}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McAllaster |first=Alan |date=November 27, 1965 |title=Big Grid Year For Tribe Forecast |work=Oakland Tribune (Oakland, California) |pages=16B}}</ref> He played at both tackle and end on the offensive line, and played more minutes than any other Stanford sophomore. He had five [[Reception (gridiron football)|pass receptions]] for 67 yards that season.<ref name=":5">{{Cite news |last=Ralston |first=John |date=August 16, 1966 |title=Ralston presents: Blaine Nye |work=Palo Alto Times (Palo Alto, California) |pages=22}}</ref> In an October 1965 game against the [[1965 Oregon Ducks football team|Oregon Ducks]], Nye caught a touchdown pass on a [[tackle-eligible play]] (one of two such touchdown plays in that game), helping Stanford upset Oregon to win, 17–14.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 11, 1965 |title=Tackle-Eligibles Help Indians Upset Oregon in PAC; 17–14 |work=Daily News-Post (Monrovia, California) |pages=8}}</ref>

As a junior, Ralston originally planned to use Nye at right offensive tackle.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Daniel |first=Bob |date=September 8, 1966 |title=From the Sidelines |work=Citizen News (Hollywood, California) |pages=B-3}}</ref> He believed Nye had the strength and speed to become a top offensive tackle, while recognizing Nye had the ability to fill in at other positions if necessary; though Ralston preferred him on the offensive line.<ref name=":5" /> An early season injury affected Stanford's lineup, and after the Cardinals first game against [[1966 San Jose State Spartans football team|San Jose State]] Ralston made Nye Stanford's starting defensive left tackle.<ref>{{Cite news |date=September 21, 1966 |title=Washington named player of the week |work=Palo Alto Times (Palo Alto, California) |pages=47}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=September 21, 1966 |title=Stanford Soph Has Surgery |work=Gazette-Times (Corvallis, Oregon) |pages=16 |agency=United Press International}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1966 Stanford Cardinal Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/stanford/1966-schedule.html |access-date=2025-12-30 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> 

As a junior in 1966, Nye led the team with 104 tackles and received honorable mention [[Pac-12 Conference|All-Pac-8]] honors.{{citation needed|date=December 2025}} [[United Press International]] (UPI) named him All-Pacific Coast honorable mention at offensive tackle, in 1966.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 29, 1966 |title=Trojans still strong on All-Coast team |work=San Luis Obispo County Telegram-Tribune |pages=8 |agency=United Press International}}</ref> The [[Pac-12 Conference|Athletic Association of Western Universities]] (AAWU) likewise named him honorable mention All-Conference in 1966, but at defensive tackle.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 9, 1966 |title=Troy Dominates Coast All-Stars |work=San Francisco Chronicle |pages=54}}</ref> As a junior, he missed two or three games with a leg injury, before rejoining the team at defensive tackle.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 9, 1966 |title=Cal. Back Hurt Out For Season |work=San Francisco Chronicle |pages=55}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=West |first=Eddie |date=November 10, 1966 |title=West Winds, The Stanford Story |work=The Register (Santa Ana, California) |pages=B14}}</ref>

As a senior in [[1967 Stanford Indians football team|1967]], UPI named Nye first-team All-Pacific Eight Conference at defensive tackle.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 6, 1967 |title=Beban Heads AAWU Team |work=The Times (San Mateo, California) |pages=38 |agency=United Press International}}</ref> The [[Associated Press]] (AP) named him an honorable mention All-American.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 8, 1967 |title=Complete Grid Selections |work=The Idaho Daily-Statesman (Boise, Idaho) |pages=5-C |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> Nye also was honorable mention All-AAWU in 1967.<ref name="fortes" /> He was named Northern California's top defensive lineman in 1967.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 30, 1967 |title=Beban Gets '2nd Chance' Today In East-West Game |work=Anaheim Bulletin (Anaheim, California) |pages=C1}}</ref> In the  December 1967 [[Hula Bowl]], Nye was a starting defensive end for the South college all-stars.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 20, 1967 |title=Beban heads Hula South squad |work=Honolulu Star-Bulletin |pages=C-8}}</ref> That same December, he also was a starting defensive tackle in the [[East West Shrine Game]] in [[San Francisco]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 5, 1967 |title=West Shrine Selections Announced |work=The Waco News-Tribune (Waco, Texas) |pages=2-B |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

Nye earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[physics]] from Stanford.<ref name=fortes>{{cite magazine |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1990/11/19/physics-and-football-were-his-fortes-blaine-nye-was-always-a-standout-student |title=Physics and football were his fortes |magazine=Sports Illustrated |last=Noland |first=Dave |date=November 19, 1990 |page=140| access-date=March 16, 2023}}</ref> He also played [[Rugby football|rugby]] at Stanford.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Blaine Nye - 1967-68 - Men's Rugby |url=https://stanfordclubsports.com/sports/mens-rugby/roster/blaine-nye/4488 |access-date=2025-04-07 |website=Stanford Recreation |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Johnson |first=Pitch |date=January 8, 1965 |title=Injuns host rugby clinic Saturday |work=Palo Alto Times (Palo Alto, California) |pages=25}}</ref>

==Professional career==
Nye was selected by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft#Round five|fifth round]] (130th overall) of the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft]] as a [[defensive tackle]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968/draft.htm |access-date=2025-04-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Nye played in 27 games during his first two seasons with the Cowboys (1968 and 1969), but did not start any games.<ref name=":6" /> He barely made the team as a rookie guard in 1968. Most of his play was on [[American football positions#Special teams|special teams]] during those two seasons, playing guard for only a half-dozen plays in two years.<ref name=":7">{{Cite news |last=Gustkey |first=Earl |date=December 21, 1973 |title=Blain Nye: Dallas' Cool Intellect |work=The Los Angeles Times |pages=12, Part III}}</ref> 

Although Nye had played principally at defensive tackle his last two years at Stanford, in drafting him the Cowboys believed that he lacked the speed and quickness to play on defense. They instead believed he could become an offensive guard in the NFL. Cowboys' offensive line coach [[Jack Myers (American football)|Jack Myers]] said Nye's high intelligence, along with his great strength and balance were the qualities the team saw that led them to this conclusion; and in fact, those qualities later made Nye a successful guard for the Cowboys. Myers also found that the coaches never had to repeat themselves with Nye, he did not make mistakes, and he was highly consistent as a player.<ref name=":7" /> 

In 1968 and 1969, [[John Wilbur (American football)|John Wilbur]] had been the Cowboys' starting right guard.<ref>{{Cite web |title=John Wilbur Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WilbJo20.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Wilbur was a 1966 Stanford graduate, and had been Nye’s college teammate.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Loverro |first=Thom |date=January 6, 2014 |title=Remembering an American original in former Redskin John Wilbur |url=https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2014/jan/6/loverro-remembering-american-original-former-redsk/ |access-date=2025-04-07 |website=The Washington Times |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1965 Stanford Cardinal Roster |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/stanford/1965-roster.html |access-date=2025-04-07 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Going into the 1970 season, the Cowboys planned to move 1969 All-Pro [[Ralph Neely]] from tackle to guard and move future Hall of Fame tackle [[Rayfield Wright]]<ref name=":8" /> into Neely's old tackle spot. Originally, Wilbur and 1969 All-Pro guard [[John Niland (American football)|John Niland]] were available to play the other guard position, with [[Tony Liscio]] to play the other tackle position.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 22, 1970 |title=Dallas Still Fights For 'Big One' |work=Green Bay Press-Gazette (Green Bay , Wisconsin) |pages=B-1 |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> Coach [[Tom Landry]] traded Wilbur to the [[1970 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]] in late August, before the season started, intending to start Wright and Liscio at tackle and Neely and Niland at guard.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Fite |first=Ed |date=August 26, 1970 |title=Dallas Cowboys hope to rope Super Bowl berth |work=The Columbus Telegram (Columbus, Nebraska) |pages=25 |agency=United Press International}}</ref><ref name="wghrev">{{cite news |last=Buttram |first=Bill |date=January 3, 1973 |title=Wilbur gets his revenge |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=xQBOAAAAIBAJ&pg=1519%2C3474065 |access-date=March 16, 2023 |newspaper=Free Lance-Star |location=Fredericksburg, Virginia |page=8}}</ref>  

Early in the [[1970 Dallas Cowboys season|1970 season]], Neely was injured. Landry chose Nye to replace Neely as the Cowboys' starting right guard. Tackle Liscio was subsequently injured, and once Neely recovered he was used at tackle to replace Liscio, with Nye remaining as a starting guard.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=1970 Dallas Cowboys Roster & Players |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/dal/1970_roster.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Nye started 12 games that season, and went on to start every Cowboys' game at right guard from 1971 through 1976, when he retired.<ref name=":6" /> In [[1970 NFL season|1970]], Nye played between Wright at tackle<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Rayfield Wright {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/rayfield-wright/ |access-date=2025-04-08 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> and [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] [[Dave Manders]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1970 Dallas Cowboys Roster & Players |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/dal/1970_roster.htm |access-date=2025-04-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Nye played next to Wright for the remainder of  Nye's career.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rayfield Wright Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WrigRa01.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In 1971, Neely went to left tackle where he was a Cowboys starter until he retired in 1977; and Niland remained the team's starting left guard from 1971 to 1975.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ralph Neely Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/N/NeelRa00.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=John Niland Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/N/NilaJo00.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

In 1970, the Cowboys led the NFL in total [[Carry (gridiron football)|rushing yardage]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1970 NFL Standings & Team Stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1970/index.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> After winning the first [[National Football Conference]] (NFC) championship after the 1970 season,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Championship - Dallas Cowboys at San Francisco 49ers - January 3rd, 1971 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197101030sfo.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> the Cowboys reached [[Super Bowl V]] on January 17, 1971, losing to the [[1970 Baltimore Colts season|Baltimore Colts]], 16–13. Nye started at right guard in the Super Bowl.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl V - Dallas Cowboys vs. Baltimore Colts - January 17th, 1971 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197101170clt.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The Cowboys reached the [[Super Bowl VI|Super Bowl]] again the following season, this time defeating the Miami Dolphins, 24–3.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl VI - Dallas Cowboys vs. Miami Dolphins - January 16th, 1972 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197201160dal.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In 1971, they had led the NFL in points scored and total yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1971 NFL Standings & Team Stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1971/index.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In Super Bowl VI, the Cowboys had 252 rushing yards against the Dolphins, often gained behind the "devastating sweeps" of Nye and Niland; bringing the two guards to national attention.<ref name=":7" /> 

In [[1972 NFL season|1972]], Nye was named to the first-team [[Newspaper Enterprise Association]] (NEA) [[All-Pro]] team.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1972 NFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1972/allpro.htm |access-date=2025-04-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The 1972 Cowboys went to the [[1972–73 NFL playoffs|NFC championship]], losing to the [[1972 Washington Redskins season|Washington]], 26–3; again with Nye at starting right guard.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1972 Dallas Cowboys Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/dal/1972.htm |access-date=2025-12-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In the 1973 season, the Cowboys once again reached the [[1973–74 NFL playoffs|NFC championship game]], losing to the [[1973 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]], 27–10. Once more Nye started at right guard.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFC Championship - Minnesota Vikings at Dallas Cowboys - December 30th, 1973 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197312300dal.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Nye was selected to play in the [[1974 Pro Bowl]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1974 NFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1974/probowl.htm |access-date=2025-04-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The following season (1974), the Cowboys missed the playoffs,<ref>{{Cite web |title=1974 Dallas Cowboys Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/dal/1974.htm |access-date=2025-12-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> but still led the NFL in total yards and rushing yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1974 NFL Standings & Team Stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1974/index.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> They reached the Super Bowl again in the 1975 season, losing [[Super Bowl X]] to the Pittsburgh Steelers, 21–17; Nye starting in his final Super Bowl appearance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1975 Dallas Cowboys Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/dal/1975.htm |access-date=2025-12-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl X - Dallas Cowboys vs. Pittsburgh Steelers - January 18th, 1976 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197601180dal.htm |access-date=2025-12-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> 

In [[1976 NFL season|1976]], Nye's final season, he was named to the All-NFC team and the [[Pro Bowl]]. The January 17, 1977 Pro Bowl game would be his last game in the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1976 NFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1976/allpro.htm |access-date=2025-04-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1976 NFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1976/probowl.htm |access-date=2025-04-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=January 18, 1977 |title=Steelers 'Steal' The NFC Blind |work=Post-Bulletin (Rochester, Minnesota) |pages=23}}</ref> Nye announced his retirement on July 23, [[1977 NFL season|1977]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/29958848/ | newspaper=The Ogden Standard-Examiner | title=Blaine Nye Is Retiring | date=July 24, 1977 | page=29 | access-date=March 16, 2023}}</ref> He was replaced by [[Tom Rafferty]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1977 Dallas Cowboys Roster & Players |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/dal/1977_roster.htm |access-date=2025-04-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

== Legacy and honors ==
During his seven years as a starting guard (1970–1976) Nye helped anchor a dominant [[offensive line]] that led the Cowboys to five NFC championship games and three [[Super Bowl]]s.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":10" /><ref name=":12" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Spagnola |first=Mickey |title=For All The Skill Players, Cowboys’ Offensive Success Relies On The ‘Engine’ |url=https://www.dallascowboys.com/news/for-all-the-skill-players-cowboys-offensive-success-relies-on-the-engine-443676 |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=www.dallascowboys.com |language=en-US}}</ref> He played in 125 games during his nine-year career with the Cowboys, starting 96. He played all of his games under future Hall of Fame head coach Tom Landry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tom Landry Record, Statistics, and Category Ranks |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/LandTo0.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Tom Landry {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/tom-landry |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> Jim Myers was Nye's offensive line coach during his first two seasons, and then Nye's [[offensive coordinator]] for the remainder of Nye's career.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jim Myers Record, Statistics, and Category Ranks |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/MyerJi0.htm |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> 

Nye was widely considered one of the smartest players in the NFL. Amidst the time and pressure of regular-season play, he earned two master's degrees. Inside the team, he founded the "Zero Club", which prided itself on performing behind the scenes. Its first rule, "Thou Shalt Not Seek Publicity", kept its members (Nye, [[Larry Cole]], and [[Pat Toomay]]) out of the limelight.<ref name="tbdisth">{{cite news |last=Chick |first=Bob |date=October 4, 1977 |title=To be dull is the thing |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=22ZQAAAAIBAJ&pg=4945%2C597602 |access-date=March 16, 2023 |newspaper=St. Petersburg Independent |location=Florida |page=1C}}</ref><ref name="colelime">{{cite news |date=March 28, 1981 |title=Cole steps into limelight with retirement |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ol0zAAAAIBAJ&pg=5099%2C554088 |access-date=March 16, 2023 |newspaper=The Bulletin |location=Bend, Oregon |page=24 |agency=UPI}}</ref> Although he did not seek publicity, he is also known for providing some of the team's famous quotes:
* "Offensive linemen are like [[salt]]. Nobody ever remembers the brand they buy".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Blaine Nye Quote: “Offensive linemen are like salt. Nobody ever remembers the brand they buy.” |url=https://quotefancy.com/quote/1765846/Blaine-Nye-Offensive-linemen-are-like-salt-Nobody-ever-remembers-the-brand-they-buy |access-date=2025-04-07 |website=quotefancy.com |language=en}}</ref>
* After [[Clint Longley]]'s famous comeback win over the [[1974 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]] on [[Thanksgiving]] Day in [[1974 Dallas Cowboys season|1974]], a reporter asked him what the game meant, his answer was "This game represents the triumph of the uncluttered mind".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Greatest 25: The Mad Bomber Strikes, 1974 |url=https://www.dallascowboys.com/news/greatest-25-the-mad-bomber-strikes-1974-326911 |access-date=2025-04-07 |website=www.dallascowboys.com |language=en-US}}</ref> 
Nye was inducted into the [[Stanford Cardinal|Stanford Athletic Hall of Fame]], named first-team on the Stanford All-Century Football Team (1991) and inducted into the Orange County Sports Hall of Fame.<ref name="servhsasp" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Penner |first=Mike |date=November 16, 1983 |title=The County's Biggest Star Wore One On His Helmet |work=The Los Angeles Times |pages=10, Part III}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Willse |first=Hudson |date=January 9, 1992 |title=Pete, Pat picks for All-Cardinals |work=The Montana Standard (Butte, Montana) |pages=9}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=November 24, 1991 |title=Plunkett elected as Stanford's Player of the Century |work=Oakland Tribune |pages=C-3}}</ref>

==Personal life==
During the offseasons, Nye earned a [[Master of Science|M.S.]] in physics from the [[University of Washington]] in [[Seattle]] in 1970, and an [[Master of Business Administration|M.B.A.]] from [[Stanford Graduate School of Business|Stanford University]] in 1974.<ref name=athchgsb>{{cite journal |url=https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/experience/news-history/history/stanford-gsb-athletic-champions |journal=Stanford Business |title=Stanford GSB Athletic Champions |date=September 25, 1980 | access-date=March 16, 2023}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> After retiring from football in 1976, he earned a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in finance from Stanford in 1981. His dissertation was titled "Demand and Pricing for Health Care and Guaranteed Insurability".<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Noland |first=Dave |date=November 19, 1990 |title=Blaine Nye Was Always A Standout Student |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1990/11/19/physics-and-football-were-his-fortes-blaine-nye-was-always-a-standout-student |journal=Sports Illustrated}}</ref>

In 1981, Nye founded Stanford Consulting Group, Inc.<ref name=scgrp>{{cite web |url=https://www.scginc.com/ |publisher=Stanford Consulting Group |title=Experts |access-date=March 16, 2023}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> He performs numerous economic analyses and research, and provides expert testimony in multiple areas including securities litigation, intellectual property, business litigation, damages, and insurance economics.<ref name="scgrp" />

His son Blaine played college football at the [[United States Air Force Academy]] and his son Zachary played college football at [[Princeton University]], both at offensive tackle.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Herrin |first=Rick |date=November 9, 2005 |title=Former guard now fights his battles in courtroom |work=Fort Worth Star-Telegram |pages=5-B}}</ref> Zachary went on to earn a Ph. D., and to work with Nye at the Stanford Consulting Group.<ref name="scgrp" />

'''Billy Dean Waddy''' (February 19, 1954 – January 21, 2022) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who played [[wide receiver]] for seven seasons for the [[Los Angeles Rams]] and the [[Minnesota Vikings]].

Waddy was a legitimate deep threat, who averaged 16.4 yards per catch over the course of his career.  Relying on his speed and agility, Billy made big plays in one of the most significant games of his career—the Rams' shocking 21–19 upset of Dallas in the 1979 divisional playoffs, where he scored a game-winning 50-yard TD with just over two minutes to play.

Several weeks later, in [[Super Bowl XIV]] against Pittsburgh, the threat of him getting open deep down the field was a constant concern to the Steelers' defensive coaches—and for good reason, as he caught three passes for 75 yards, including a 50-yard completion from quarterback [[Vince Ferragamo]].  Late in the fourth quarter, with the Rams trailing 24–19, Waddy was wide open, streaking down the left side of the field on a play where the inexperienced Rams quarterback could not spot him, and threw an interception underneath in the middle of the field, essentially ending Los Angeles' chances in the 31–19 loss.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XIV - Los Angeles Rams vs. Pittsburgh Steelers - January 20th, 1980 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198001200pit.htm |access-date=2022-05-20 |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Sabol |first=Steve |title=Official Film of Super Bowl XIV |url=http://NFL.com |publisher=NFL Films |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20101127184026/http://nfl.com/ |archivedate=November 27, 2010 }}</ref>

He died in [[New Brighton, Minnesota]], on January 21, 2022, at the age of 67.<ref>{{cite news |title=Billy Waddy |url=https://www.washburn-mcreavy.com/obituaries/Billy-Waddy/#!/Obituary |access-date=February 2, 2022 |publisher=Washburn McReavy}}</ref>

'''William Dean Shields''' (born August 23, 1954) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily for the  [[San Diego Chargers]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football|Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets]] and was selected by the Chargers in the sixth round of the [[1975 NFL draft]].  Shields also played in the NFL for the [[San Francisco 49ers]], [[New York Jets]] and [[Kansas City Chiefs]].

==College career==
Shields played [[college football]] at [[Georgia Tech]] from 1972 to 1974. He was inducted into the Georgia Tech Hall of Fame in 1985.<ref>{{cite web |title=Georgia Tech Hall of Fame |url=https://ramblinwreck.com/georgia-tech-sports-hall-of-fame/##fb|website=Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets|date=July 27, 2018 }}</ref>

==Professional career==
===San Diego Chargers===
Shields was selected by the [[San Diego Chargers]] in the sixth round of the [[1975 NFL draft]] with the 136th overall pick.<ref name="CBS">{{cite news|last=Edwards|first=Josh|url=https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/draft/news/ultimate-nfl-draft-the-best-pick-for-all-256-slots-over-the-last-50-years-from-peyton-manning-to/|title=Ultimate NFL Draft: The best pick for all 256 slots over the last 50 years, from Peyton Manning to Ryan Succop|date=June 12, 2020|website=[[CBS Sports]]|access-date=May 17, 2024}}</ref> He became a starter for the team in 1976,<ref name="UPI1">{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line-->|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1984/08/10/The-San-Diego-Chargers-Friday-traded-veteran-offensive-tackle/4494460958400/|title=The San Diego Chargers Friday traded veteran offensive tackle ...|date=August 10, 1984|website=[[United Press International|UPI]]|access-date=May 17, 2024}}</ref> and started 119 games for the team.<ref name="CBS" /><ref name= "WP">{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line-->|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1984/09/28/71602b7d-2248-480f-b63e-f75f9b9aedd7/|title=Football: San Francisco 49ers|date=September 27, 1984|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=May 17, 2024}}</ref> A contract dispute between Shields and the Chargers resulted in his [[holdout (sports)|holding out]] during [[Training camp (NFL)|training camp]], and this led to the team trading him to the [[1984 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]] in August 1984.<ref name="CBS" /><ref name="UPI1" /> The Vikings, however, returned Shields to the Chargers after failing to come to contract terms with him and exercised a [[Contingent contract|contingency clause]] for draft picks instead.<ref>{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line-->|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1984/09/05/0fd417ee-bb49-4a34-b1c1-0bbb8299dcde/|title=Football: Minnesota Vikings|date=September 5, 1984|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref> Shields was waived by the Chargers a few weeks into the [[1984 NFL season|1984 season]].<ref name= "WP" />

===San Francisco 49ers===
The 49ers signed Shields off [[Waivers (NFL)|waivers]] in September 1984 to bolster the team's [[offensive line]] which had been hit by injuries to several players.<ref name= "WP" /><ref name="CW">{{cite book|last=Willis|first=Chris|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZQ4WBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA133|title=A Nearly Perfect Season: The Inside Story of the 1984 San Francisco 49ers|page=133|year=2014|publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]]|location= [[Lanham, Maryland]]|isbn=978-1-4422-3642-4|via=[[Google Books]]|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref> Shields stated that he had been in discussions with four teams before choosing the 49ers, and that his decision was mainly based on personal relationships he had with already established with some of the team's coaches and players.<ref name="CW" /> Shields was mainly a reserve{{mdash}}playing in twelve games and starting once{{mdash}}on the [[Super Bowl XIX]] winners.<ref name="UPI2">{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line-->|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/08/02/The-New-York-Jets-whose-two-starting-offensive-tackles/2840491803200/|title=The New York Jets, whose two starting offensive tackles...|date=August 2, 1985|website=UPI|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref> He was traded to the [[1985 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] for a 6th round [[draft pick]] in August 1985.<ref name="UPI2" /><ref name="NYT">{{cite news|last=Rhoden|first=William C.|author-link=William C. Rhoden|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/08/23/sports/jets-acquire-2-big-persons.html|url-access=subscription|title=Jets Acquire 2 'Big Persons'|date=August 23, 1985|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref>

===New York Jets===
Shields suffered a knee injury in the Jets' second game of the [[1985 New York Jets season#Pre season|1985 pre season]], a 24{{ndash}}20 loss to the [[1985 Cincinnati Bengals season|Cincinnati Bengals]].<ref name="NYT" /><ref>{{cite news|last=Eskenazi|first=Gerald|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/08/23/sports/jets-acquire-2-big-persons.html|url-access=subscription|title=Jets' Injury List Is Continuing to Grow|date=August 19, 1985|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref> Shields was placed on [[injured reserve]] by the team in September 1985,<ref>{{cite news|last=Yannis|first=Alex|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/09/04/sports/receivers-for-jets-an-untested-group.html|url-access=subscription|title=Receivers for Jets an Untested Group|date=September 4, 1985|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref> was reactivated in November 1985<ref>{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line-->|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/11/08/Fridays-Sports-Transactions/7902500274000/|title=Friday's Sports Transactions|date=November 8, 1985|website=UPI|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line-->|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/11/09/sports/sports-people-jets-activate-shields.html|url-access=subscription|title=Jets Activate Shields|date=November 9, 1985|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref> but was cut by the team in December 1985.<ref>{{cite news|last=Eskenazi|first=Gerald|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/12/06/sports/jets-are-successful-with-big-turnover.html|url-access=subscription|title=Jets Are Successful with Big Turnover|date=December 6, 1985|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref>

===Kansas City Chiefs===
The [[1985 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] claimed Shields off waivers from the Jets on December 7, 1985.<ref>{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line-->|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/12/07/Sports-Digest/9074502779600/|title=Sports Digest|date=December 7, 1985|website=UPI|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref>

==Personal life and post playing career==
Shields co-operated a development company in the San Diego area with former Chargers' teammate [[Don Macek]] in 1990.<ref>{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line-->|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1990/04/27/Charger-veteran-Don-Macek-retires/2974641188800/|title=Charger veteran Don Macek retires|date=April 27, 1990|website=UPI|access-date=May 18, 2024}}</ref>

Shields was a plaintiff in a 2012 lawsuit filed by former NFL player [[Brent Boyd]] against the NFL over [[Concussions in American football#Federal NFL concussion litigation|concussion related injuries]] sustained while playing.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.hausfeld.com/uploads/documents/boydamendedcomplaint.pdf|chapter-url=https://www.hausfeld.com/uploads/documents/boydamendedcomplaint.pdf#page=77|title=Brent Boyd, et al., Plaintiffs, v. National Football League, et al., Defendants|chapter=192. Plaintiff William "Billy" Shields|page=77|publisher=[[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania]]|via=Hausfeld.com|access-date=May 28, 2024|archive-date=May 20, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240520011739/https://www.hausfeld.com/uploads/documents/boydamendedcomplaint.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Winter played professionally as a [[defensive end]] for the [[Indianapolis Colts]], [[San Diego Chargers]] and [[Green Bay Packers]] on the [[National Football League]] (NFL), and coached [[college football]] for the [[UCF Knights football|UCF Knights]]. ==College career== After playing football, basketball and track at [[Tappan Zee High School]],{{cite news |title=Ex-Packer Winter back to where he once belonged |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/61213673/an-article-about-journeyman-blaise/ |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |work=Racine Journal Times |via=Newspapers.com |date=December 18, 1992}} Winter took a tour of colleges in the Northeast United States after his senior year of high school, looking for an opportunity to play college football. [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse]] was the only school to offer Winter a scholarship, and that was only after a previous commit decommitted.{{cite web |last1=Simers |first1=T. J. |title=The Line of Great Persistence : Football: After being released and rejected, Blaise Winter sold the Chargers on himself. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-09-18-sp-584-story.html |website=Los Angeles Times |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |date=September 18, 1992}} Winter was named a team captain and most valuable player during his senior season with the Orange. ==Professional career== ===Indianapolis Colts=== Winter was selected by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the second round (35th overall) of the [[1984 NFL draft]].{{Cite web |title=1984 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1984/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-10 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} He started all but one game during his rookie season, and was named to some all-rookie teams.{{cite news |last1=Daveronica |first1=Jeff |title=Winter blazing new path with Bills |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/61213110/an-article-about-then-recent-bills/ |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |work=Rochester Democrat and Chronicle |via=Newspapers.com |date=July 17, 1995}} A shoulder injury landed him on injured reserve during his sophomore season; the Colts released him at the end of the year.{{cite web |last1=Carucci |first1=Vic |title=Bills Sign Journeyman for Defensive tackle Winter Spent '94 Season on injured reserve |url=https://buffalonews.com/news/bills-sign-journeyman-for-defense-tackle-winter-spent-94-on-ir/article_c515b60e-b256-5a89-9499-486765621038.html |website=Buffalo News |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |date=June 28, 1995}} ===San Diego Chargers (first stint)=== Winter played with the [[San Diego Chargers]] during the 1987 season, which was shortened by a players strike. ===Green Bay Packers=== Winter was traded to the [[Green Bay Packers]] in early 1988 in exchange for past considerations. He started most of the 1988 and 1989 seasons, but played in a limited role in 1990 and was cut by the Packers early in the 1991 calendar year. Following his release from the team, Winter made telephone calls to every NFL team and also made a highlight reel which was shipped to every team. He started driving to team facilities in an effort to get signed, but did not draw any interest until the offseason, when the [[San Francisco 49ers]], [[Minnesota Vikings]] and [[Los Angeles Rams]] showed interest, and Winter participated in workouts for the Vikings and 49ers.{{cite web |last1=Dorman |first1=Larry |title=Winter refused to be left in the cold |url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/fl-xpm-1993-01-09-9301020630-story.html |website=South Florida Sentinel |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |date=January 9, 1993}} ===San Diego Chargers (second stint)=== Winter was signed by the San Diego Chargers in the time period preceding the [[1992 NFL draft]]. He originally sat third-string on the depth chart, but later started during the season after [[Joe Phillips (American football)|Joe Phillips]] refused to agree to a contract and [[George Thornton (American football)|George Thornton]] did not play well. He played the 1993 season before being cut by the team. ===Tampa Bay Buccaneers=== Winter was a member of the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] for a brief time in the 1994 offseason. ===San Diego Chargers (third stint)=== The Chargers brought Winter back for the 1994 season, but a cut block by [[Dave Cadigan]] of the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] tore Winter's [[anterior cruciate ligament]] in September, ending his season. ===Buffalo Bills=== Winter signed with the [[Buffalo Bills]] in spring 1995 after an onslaught of injuries to the team's defensive line, but he himself spent the year on the injured reserve list. ==After playing== Winter, his wife and children moved to [[Appleton, Wisconsin]] after his playing career ended. He wrote an autobiography, entitled "A Reason to Believe".{{cite web |title=Fear No evil - Blaise Winter |url=https://ucfknights.com/news/2012/3/9/Fear_No_Evil_Blaise_Winter.aspx |website=UCF Knights football |publisher=University of Central Florida |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |date=March 9, 2012}} The [[UCF Knights football|University of Central Florida]] hired Winter as a defensive line coach for the 2012 season.{{cite web |last1=Limón |first1=Iliana |title=UCF hires Blaise Winter to take over as defensive line coach |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/sports/ucf-knights/os-ucf-hires-blaise-winter-story.html |website=Orlando Sentinel |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |date=February 24, 2012}} Winter spent one season on the coaching staff and then departed, citing a lack of family time. After coaching, Winter became a motivational speaker. ==Personal life== Winter was born with a [[cleft palate]] and he later grew tumors in both of his ears. He dabbled in martial arts in high school.{{cite web |last1=Hendricks |first1=Martin |title=Blaise Winter now motivational speaker |url=https://archive.jsonline.com/sports/packers/blaise-winter-now-motivational-speaker-b99308760z1-267598531.html/ |website=Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |date=July 17, 2014}} Winter was diagnosed with a brain tumor in 2016.{{cite web |last1=Hays |first1=Chris |title=Former Michigan State recruit Donovan Winter recounts downward spiral, apologizes |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/sports/florida-recruiting/os-sp-donovan-winter-michigan-state-0618-story.html |website=Orlando Sentinel |accessdate=October 16, 2020 |date=June 17, 2017}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{Official website|http://www.blaisewinter.com/}} * [https://ucfknights.com/staff-directory/blaise-winter/108 UCF Knights profile] * [https://www.hearstrong.org/ambassadors/blaise-winter/ HearStrong profile] * {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060515000051/http://www.lutzagency.com/winterb.htm Lutz Agency profile]}} * [https://www.wcspeakers.com/speaker/blaise-winter/ World Class Speakers profile] {{Indianapolis Colts 1984 draft navbox}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Winter, Blaise}} [[Category:1962 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:American deaf people]] [[Category:People from Blauvelt, New York]] [[Category:Players of American football from Rockland County, New York]] [[Category:Deaf players of American football]] [[Category:American football defensive linemen]] [[Category:Syracuse Orange football players]] [[Category:Indianapolis Colts players]] [[Category:San Diego Chargers players]] [[Category:Green Bay Packers players]] [[Category:Tampa Bay Buccaneers players]] [[Category:Buffalo Bills players]] [[Category:UCF Knights football coaches]] [[Category:Finlandia Lions football coaches]]

"Jets Get 2 Saints To Help Defense," ''The New York Times'', Tuesday, January 30, 1973.] Retrieved November 1, 2020</ref><ref>[https://www.prosportstransactions.com/football/DraftTrades/Years/1973.htm 1973 NFL Draft Pick Transactions, January 30 (Rounds 1–7) & 31 (Rounds 8–17) – Pro Sports Transactions.] Retrieved November 1, 2020</ref>

Newsome died on November 12, 2024, aged 76.<ref>[https://www.mercymcgowan.com/blog/post/mr-billy-ray-newsome Mr. Billy Ray Newsome]</ref>

'''Blake Costanzo''' (born April 14, 1984) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Lafayette Leopards football|Lafayette Leopards]] and was signed by the [[New York Jets]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2006.

Costanzo was also a member of the [[Buffalo Bills]], [[Cleveland Browns]], [[San Francisco 49ers]], and [[Chicago Bears]].

==Early life==
He played [[high school football]] at [[Ramapo High School (New Jersey)|Ramapo High School]] in his [[New Jersey]] hometown as a linebacker and a tight end. He helped lead his team to two state championships. He played linebacker and tight end, and was awarded the Defensive Player of the Year Award. In his high school career, he recorded 210 tackles, 24 sacks, and 11 blocked punts. He was named three times to the All-League first-team, as well as the All-Bergen County first-team. In 2001, he was named the Defensive Player of the Year after recording 111 tackles, 15 sacks, and five blocked punts.<ref name=Lafayette>{{cite web |url=http://www.goleopards.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/costanzo_blake00.html |title=Player Bio: Blake Costanzo - Lafayette Leopards Official Athletic Site |publisher=Goleopards.com |date= |accessdate=August 1, 2012 |archive-date=July 22, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120722161227/http://www.goleopards.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/costanzo_blake00.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==College career==

===2002===
In 2002, Costanzo recorded 34 tackles and finish fourth among the Leopard freshmen in tackles. He also made two sacks, while leading the team in forced fumbles with two.<ref name=Lafayette />

===2003===
In 2003, he ranked third among the Leopards and seventh in the [[Patriot League]] with 94 total tackles. He also blocked a three kicks, and recorded 13 stops and blocked a PAT against the [[Colgate Raiders football|Colgate Raiders]]. He also recorded 12 tackles and blocked two punts against [[Towson Tigers football|Towson]]. He also recorded 12 tackles against [[Georgetown Hoyas football|Georgetown]] and [[Columbia Lions football|Columbia]], as well as recording his first career interception against [[Holy Cross Crusaders football|Holy Cross]].<ref name=Lafayette />

===2004===
In 2004, he was the team's Most Outstanding Linebacker, as he ranked second on the team and seventh in the Patriot League with 93 tackles. He had 5.5 sacks, and recorded 1.5 sacks against [[Bucknell Bison football|Bucknell]]. Against the Holy Cross Crusaders, he made 12 tackles, forced a fumble, and blocked an extra point. Against the Columbia Lions, he made 11 tackles, a sack and a fumble recovery. Against the [[Fordham Rams football|Fordham Rams]], he recorded a sack vs. Fordham, as well as blocking a fourth-quarter field goal against Colgate, along with recording a sack against [[Delaware Fightin' Blue Hens football|Delaware]].<ref name=Lafayette />

==Professional career==

===New York Jets===

Costanzo was signed as an undrafted free agent by the [[New York Jets]] in 2006, and was on the [[practice squad]] until 2007.

===Buffalo Bills===

Costanzo played for the [[Buffalo Bills]] in 2007 and 2009 seasons.

===Cleveland Browns===

In the 2010 season, Costanzo played in ten games before injuring his groin and being placed on injured reserve.<ref name=Lehigh>{{cite web|author=Photo Courtesy of Cleveland Browns |url=https://www.lehighvalleylive.com/sports/index.ssf/2011/08/blake_costanzo_signs_one-year.html |title=Blake Costanzo signs one-year deal with San Francisco 49ers |publisher=lehighvalleylive.com |date= August 4, 2011|accessdate=August 1, 2012}}</ref>

===San Francisco 49ers (first stint)===

Costanzo was signed by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in 2011.<ref name=Lehigh /> Costanzo was notable for forcing a fumble in the [[2011–12 NFL playoffs]] against the [[New Orleans Saints]] on a kickoff and recovering another, en route to a 49ers 36–32 victory.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lafayette.edu/about/news/2012/01/16/blake-costanzo-%E2%80%9906-helps-49ers-advance-to-nfc-championship-game/ |title=Blake Costanzo '06 Helps 49ers Advance to NFC Championship Game · About · Lafayette College |publisher=Lafayette.edu |accessdate=August 1, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121219055655/http://www.lafayette.edu/about/news/2012/01/16/blake-costanzo-%e2%80%9906-helps-49ers-advance-to-nfc-championship-game/ |archive-date=December 19, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 61 career games, Costanzo has recorded 71 tackles on special teams with eight forced fumble/fumble recoveries (four force fumbles, four fumble recoveries). In the 2011 season, Costanzo recorded 17 special teams tackles, which ranks second on the 49ers.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/DailyBlogs.asp?DAILY_BLOG_DATE=07/31/12 |title=Bears a special team for Costanzo |publisher=Chicagobears.com |accessdate=August 1, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120802003926/http://www.chicagobears.com/DailyBlogs.asp?DAILY_BLOG_DATE=07%2F31%2F12 |archive-date=August 2, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Chicago Bears===

Costanzo was signed by the [[Chicago Bears]] in 2012 on a two-year deal.<ref>{{cite news|title=Bears sign veteran linebacker Blake Costanzo|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2012/03/13/bears-sign-veteran-linebacker-blake-costanzo/|date=March 13, 2012|author=Brad Biggs|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|access-date=March 22, 2012}}</ref> General manager [[Phil Emery (American football)|Phil Emery]] commented, "Blake has done some dynamic things as a special teams player, as is evident from his four forced fumbles with one of them in a playoff game against New Orleans this past year."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=8698 |title=Bears fill key needs, bolster their roster |publisher=Chicagobears.com |date=March 20, 2012 |accessdate=August 1, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120605020058/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=8698 |archive-date=June 5, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Costanzo ended the 2013 season leading the Bears with 17 special teams tackles.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chicagobears.com/multimedia/photo-gallery/2013-Season-Highlights/63dcadad-fea7-4e96-b6ee-9c8374fd01b0|title=2013 Season Highlights|work=[[Chicago Bears]]|date=January 8, 2014|accessdate=January 8, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140109015340/http://www.chicagobears.com/multimedia/photo-gallery/2013-Season-Highlights/63dcadad-fea7-4e96-b6ee-9c8374fd01b0|archive-date=January 9, 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===San Francisco 49ers (second stint)===

On June 3, 2014, Costanzo signed a one-year deal to return to the 49ers. He was released later in the year.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Adams |first=Luke |date=June 3, 2014 |title=49ers Sign Blake Costanzo |url=https://www.profootballrumors.com/2014/06/49ers-sign-blake-costanzo |access-date=2025-01-29 |website=Pro Football Rumors |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Blair Armstrong Kiel''' (November 29, 1961 – April 8, 2012) was an American professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL), and [[Arena Football League]] (AFL). He was a four-year [[Starting lineup|starting]] quarterback and [[punter (gridiron football)|punter]] in [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]] from 1980 to 1983.  He was inducted into the [[Indiana Football Hall of Fame]] in 1998.

==College career==
Kiel attended [[Columbus East High School]] in [[Indiana]], where he was rated the #3 quarterback in the nation by ''[[Parade (magazine)|Parade]]''.  Coach [[Dan Devine]] offered him a [[scholarship]] to the [[University of Notre Dame]], where Kiel earned the starting quarterback job during his freshman year, four games into the 1980 season.  The team achieved a 9-0-1 record and the #2 ranking before closing the season with losses at [[USC Trojans football|USC]] (3-20) and to [[Georgia Bulldogs football|Georgia]] in the [[Sugar Bowl]] (10–17).

Kiel went on to become the sixth all-time leading passer for Notre Dame, and holds the record for the team's longest pass play—a 96-yard bomb to Joe Howard against [[Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football|Georgia Tech]] in 1981.  In his final game, he led his unranked team to victory over 13th-ranked [[Boston College]] in the [[Liberty Bowl]].

==Professional career==
Kiel was selected 281st overall in the 11th round by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the [[1984 NFL draft]] but only saw playing time in the regular season as a [[Holder (American football)|holder]] on kick attempts.  He later played in seven games over two seasons with the [[Indianapolis Colts]] as both a quarterback and [[Punter (American football)|punter]], and then spent three years with the [[Green Bay Packers]].  Following stints in the [[Canadian Football League]] and the [[Arena Football League (1987–2008)|Arena Football League]], he retired at the end of 1993.

==Personal life==
After retirement, Kiel resided in the Fishers area and worked as a private quarterback coach. He died of a heart attack at Columbus Regional Hospital on April 8, 2012, at the age of 50.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.therepublic.com/view/local_story/Ex_East_Notre_Dame_star_Blair__1333937134/|title=Ex-East, Notre Dame Star Blair Kiel Dies at 50|work=The Republic|date=April 8, 2012|access-date=April 9, 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120411205113/http://www.therepublic.com/view/local_story/Ex_East_Notre_Dame_star_Blair__1333937134|archive-date=April 11, 2012}}</ref>

Kiel's nephew, [[Gunner Kiel]], played college football for Notre Dame and [[Cincinnati Bearcats football|Cincinnati]]. His brother, Kip, played for [[Butler Bulldogs football|Butler]]; another nephew, Drew, played at [[Illinois State Redbirds football|Illinois State]]; a third nephew, Dusty, played at [[Indiana Hoosiers football|Indiana]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Long |first=Corey |date=April 27, 2011 |title= Gunner Kiel gets home schooled |website=[[ESPN]] |url=https://www.espn.com/college-sports/recruiting/football/news/story?id=6437646 |access-date=February 29, 2024}}</ref>

'''Willie Perry Milner''' (born June 21, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[Tackle (American football)#Offensive tackle|offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He attended Northside High School in Atlanta. Milner attended the [[University of Houston]],<ref>{{cite news|title=Dolphins sign No. 1 pick|work=Beaver County Times|date=1995-07-18|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=FCJVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=hDsNAAAAIBAJ&pg=5546,3627884|accessdate=2011-02-07}}</ref> where he was a third-team college All-American and the team's MVP. He was selected 25th in the first round of the [[1995 NFL draft]] by the [[Miami Dolphins]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1995 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1995/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He started 9 games as a rookie,<ref>{{cite web|title=Billy Milner|publisher=Pro Football Reference|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/MilnBi21.htm|accessdate=2011-02-07}}</ref> earning a spot on the all rookie team. He was traded to the [[St. Louis Rams]] his second season for tight end [[Troy Drayton]]<ref>{{cite news|last=Bricker|first=Charles|title=Dolphins Acquire Tight End, Cut Byars|work=Orlando Sentinel|date=1996-10-02|url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1996/10/02/dolphins-acquire-tight-end-cut-byars/|access-date=2011-02-07}}</ref> and suffered a career ending neck injury in his third season derailing a promising career. Milner now resides in [[Sunrise, Florida]], with his wife Sabrina and daughter Breana, he also has a son (Maxwell) who lives in [[Houston]], [[Texas]].{{citation needed|date=February 2014}}

'''Billy Taylor''' (born July 6, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was selected by the [[New York Giants]] in the fourth round of the [[1978 NFL draft]]. A 6'0", 215-lb. running back from [[Texas Tech University|Texas Tech]], Taylor played for five [[NFL]] seasons as a [[running back]] and [[kick returner]]. He spent his first three seasons as a member of the Giants, and spent his final two split between the Giants, the [[New York Jets]], and the [[Los Angeles Raiders]]. As the starting running back for the Giants, he led the team in rushing in [[1979 NFL season|1979]] and [[1980 NFL season|1980]]. His best season was in [[1979 New York Giants season|1979]], when he started all 16 games, carrying the ball 198 times for 700 yards and catching it another 28 times for 253 yards with 11 total touchdowns. The Jets picked him up after the Giants waived him in [[1981 NFL season|1981]], but they cut him three weeks later when they needed to add a defensive lineman to replace the injured [[Marty Lyons]].<ref>Wire Reports. "Jets Drop Taylor". St. Petersburg Times. 28 Oct 1981</ref> Taylor then played two seasons for the Washington Federals of the [[United States Football League|USFL]], amassing 171 rushes for 757 yards and 5 touchdowns along with 64 receptions for 523 yards and 2 touchdowns in 1983. In 1984, Taylor rushed 142 times for 499 yards while also collecting 51 receptions for 387 yards and a touchdown.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.kendrick.org/(X(1)S(1zmzzdf3itwxftadczmfplfl))/Federals?AspxAutoDetectCookieSupport=1|title=Washington Federals|website=www.kendrick.org|access-date=2019-05-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191214130225/http://www.kendrick.org/(X(1)S(1zmzzdf3itwxftadczmfplfl))/Federals?AspxAutoDetectCookieSupport=1|archive-date=2019-12-14|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Taylor went on to become a corporate trainer for Hunter Douglas, and involved with charities.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://archive.stjohns.edu/pls/portal30/sportdev.redstormsports.show_left_html?sec_id%3D1069%26category%3DREDSTORMSPORTS+HOME%26html_source%3D2288 |title=St John's University Athletic Department - Home Page |accessdate=2009-05-09 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716054934/http://archive.stjohns.edu/pls/portal30/sportdev.redstormsports.show_left_html?sec_id=1069&category=REDSTORMSPORTS%20HOME&html_source=2288 |archivedate=2011-07-16 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.prosportsexperience.com/new-york-heroes/|title=New York NFL Alumni Hero Youth Football Camps|website=Pro Sports Experience|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-29}}</ref> Billy Taylor was a successful broadcast journalist after playing football. This included stints with TV and radio. Most notably he co-hosted with Larry Hardesty on WLIB a talk show which had good success as the only minority talk show in New York City Area.

'''Bivian Lewis Lee Jr.''' (August 3, 1948 – November 14, 1984<ref name="Lee dies">{{cite web |date=November 14, 1984 |title=SPORTS NEWS BRIEFS; Lee, an Ex-Back For Saints, Dies |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/11/14/sports/sports-news-briefs-lee-an-ex-back-for-saints-dies.html |access-date=April 11, 2026 |website=The New York Times |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). The [[New Orleans Saints]] selected him in the third round of the [[1971 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] at [[Prairie View A&M Panthers|Prairie View A&M]].

Lee played quarterback at [[Emile High School]] in [[Bastrop, Texas]]. He went to Prairie View, where he remains the record-holder for 21 career interceptions. He also returned one interception 105 yards for a score.<ref name="Bivian Lee's legacy">{{Cite web|url=http://www.statesman.com/news/local/bivian-lee-legacy-goes-beyond-football/sRPON4OHwBVjZmELQZ81CM/|title=Bivian Lee's legacy goes beyond football}}{{Dead link|date=March 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

Lee led the Saints in interceptions with four in 1972 and was tied for the team lead with three in 1973.<ref name="Lee dies" />

He died of [[cardiac arrhythmia]], with his death providing some impetus for congressional investigations into dietary supplements.<ref name="Bivian Lee's legacy" />

His son, Bivian "Sonny" Lee III, was honored during the 15th Annual BET Awards for his work as the founder of Son of a Saint, a 501 c 3 organization based in New Orleans that mentors boys whose fathers have been incarcerated or are dead.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.uno.edu/campus-news/2015/UNO-Alumnus-Bivian-Sonny-Lee-III-Receives-BET-2015-Shine-a-Light-Award.aspx |title=UNO Alumnus Bivian "Sonny" Lee III Receives BET's 2015 Shine a Light Award | University of New Orleans |access-date=2017-10-24 |archive-date=2017-10-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171024205318/http://www.uno.edu/campus-news/2015/UNO-Alumnus-Bivian-Sonny-Lee-III-Receives-BET-2015-Shine-a-Light-Award.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref>

'''William James Parks''' (January 1, 1948 – July 22, 2009) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[San Diego Chargers]], [[Dallas Cowboys]], and [[Houston Oilers]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Long Beach State 49ers football|Long Beach State 49ers]].

==Early life==
Parks attended [[Culver City High School]], where he played [[quarterback]] and [[defensive back]]. He moved on to [[Santa Monica College]], where he was moved to [[wide receiver]] after suffering a preseason concussion.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.sgvtribune.com/2009/07/23/krikorian-parks-is-hailed-as-eccentric-delightful/| title=Parks is hailed as eccentric, delightful | publisher=The San Gabriel Valley Tribune | date=August 30, 2017 | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> In 1966, he set a school record with 9 [[touchdown]] receptions in a season.

In 1967, he transferred to [[Long Beach State University]], where he became the school's first [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]]. He had his best season as a sophomore, catching 79 passes (second in the nation) for 1,294 yards and 12 touchdowns. He was named All-American in 1968 as a junior, but was injured much of his senior year.

Parks holds the school marks for receiving yards in a career (2,919), receiving yards in a game (298, versus [[UCSB]] in 1968), yards in a season (1,294 in 1967) and career [[touchdown]]s (22). He also recorded 169 career receptions.

In 1986, he was inducted into the Long Beach State University Hall of Fame.

==Professional career==

===San Diego Chargers===
Parks was selected by the [[San Diego Chargers]] in the 6th round (146th overall) of the [[1970 NFL draft]]. He sat the entire [[1970 NFL season|1970 season]] because of injuries.

In [[1971 NFL season|1971]], he replaced [[Lance Alworth]] in the lineup and led the [[NFL]] in catches (41 catches) during the first ten games of the season, before being sidelined with a broken arm he suffered in the 10th game. He was named to the [[1971 NFL season|1971]] [[NFL]] All-rookie team.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1798&dat=19711221&id=UyAeAAAAIBAJ&sjid=H40EAAAAIBAJ&pg=3635,4052148 | title=Plunkett & Vataha On All-Rookie Team | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

In [[1972 NFL season|1972]], the Chargers coveted [[running back]] [[Duane Thomas]], the team traded Parks along with [[running back]] [[Mike Montgomery (American football)|Mike Montgomery]] to the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in exchange for him on August 1.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.si.com/vault/1972/09/18/614373/national-east| title=National East | publisher=Sports Illustrated| date=September 18, 1972 | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

===Dallas Cowboys===
In [[1972 NFL season|1972]] he was a backup [[wide receiver]] until the eighth game, when he was promoted to replace [[Lance Alworth]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2519&dat=19721030&id=2M5dAAAAIBAJ&sjid=b14NAAAAIBAJ&pg=3129,4945723 | title=Alworth, Hayes Benched For Test Against Lions | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> He would have a disappointing regular season with only 18 receptions, but he was a key player in the come from behind win over the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in the playoffs, catching 7 passes for 136 yards and a [[touchdown]], in what turned out to be his best game as a professional.

Parks was traded along with [[Tody Smith]] before the start of the [[1973 NFL season|1973 season]] to the [[Houston Oilers]], in exchange for their first and third round draft picks in the [[1974 NFL draft]]. For the first time in their history, the [[Dallas Cowboys]] had the first overall draft choice which they used to select [[Ed "Too Tall" Jones]]. The team used the third round draft choice to select [[Danny White]].

===Houston Oilers===
During his first season with the Oilers in [[1973 NFL season|1973]], he had a career-high of 43 catches. He grabbed another 20 passes in [[1974 NFL season|1974]], but only caught 1 pass in 10 games in [[1975 NFL season|1975]].

Parks retired after the [[1975 NFL season|1975 season]] having played in the [[NFL]] for 5 seasons. He caught 123 passes for 1,826 yards and 7 [[touchdown]]s in his career.

==Personal life==
Parks succumbed to [[melanoma]] at age 61 in Hawaii.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.longbeachstate.com/trads/hof/parks-billy.html | title=Billy Parks Hall of Fame bio | publisher=Long Beach State University Athletics Website | accessdate=February 19, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180114070147/http://www.longbeachstate.com/trads/hof/parks-billy.html | archive-date=January 14, 2018 | url-status=dead }}</ref>
